title: Find every cut vertex in one pass
description:
A vertex of an undirected graph is a cut vertex when deleting it, together with every edge that touches it, leaves the graph in more separate pieces than it was in before.

Implement a function called ArticulationPoints that receives the number of vertices and an adjacency list, and returns every cut vertex of that graph in ascending order. Vertices are numbered from zero. The adjacency list gives, for each vertex, the vertices it shares an edge with; every edge appears in both directions.

ArticulationPoints(5, [[1, 2, 3], [0, 2], [0, 1], [0, 4], [3]]) -> [0, 3]. That graph is a triangle on 0, 1, 2 with a tail 0 - 3 - 4: deleting 0 strands the pair 1, 2 from the pair 3, 4, and deleting 3 strands 4 on its own, while deleting any other vertex leaves one connected piece.

A graph with no cut vertex returns an empty list. A four-vertex ring is the smallest example: ArticulationPoints(4, [[1, 3], [0, 2], [1, 3], [0, 2]]) -> [].

The hidden tests hold you to three more things. The graph is not guaranteed to be connected, so every piece of it has to be examined, not just the piece the first vertex is in. A vertex with no edges at all is never a cut vertex, because deleting it leaves the rest of the graph exactly as it was. And the returned list is always sorted ascending, whatever order you happen to discover the vertices in.

This card asks for the optimal solution, and the tests enforce it: one of them is a graph of over a hundred thousand vertices with a two second budget. Deleting one vertex at a time and recounting the pieces gives the right answer but is far too slow to pass. The whole graph has to be settled in a single traversal that visits each vertex and each edge once, in time proportional to their total.
objective: Recall and implement the linear-time, single-traversal algorithm for finding the cut vertices of an undirected graph.

title: Order a DAG so every edge points forward
description:
A directed graph is in topological order when every edge points forward: for an edge from u to v, u sits somewhere before v in the list. Reading the order left to right is reading a set of tasks in an order that never starts one before something it depends on is finished.

Implement a function called TopologicalOrder that receives the number of vertices and an adjacency list, and returns a topological order of that graph. Vertices are numbered from zero. The adjacency list gives, for each vertex, the vertices its outgoing edges point at, so entry u holding [1, 3] means there is an edge from u to 1 and an edge from u to 3.

TopologicalOrder(6, [[1], [2], [3], [], [5], [1, 2]]) -> [0, 4, 5, 1, 2, 3]. Those are the edges 0 -> 1, 1 -> 2, 2 -> 3, 4 -> 5, 5 -> 1 and 5 -> 2, and in that list every one of them points forward. Most graphs have more than one valid answer, and this one is no exception: [4, 5, 0, 1, 2, 3] is just as correct. The hidden tests check the rule, not one particular list, so any ordering containing all the vertices with no edge pointing backwards passes.

A graph with no edges at all puts no constraint on anything, so any arrangement of its vertices is an answer, as long as every vertex is in it.

Only a graph without cycles can be ordered this way, and the tests give you cyclic ones. When no topological order exists, return an empty list rather than a partial ordering. A vertex with an edge to itself counts as a cycle, and so does a cycle sitting in a part of the graph that nothing else points into. A graph with zero vertices is not a failure; its answer is the empty list too.

How you get there is yours to choose, but it has to be efficient, and the tests enforce it: one of them is a graph of two hundred thousand vertices and twice as many edges, with a two second budget. Rescanning every remaining vertex to find the next one that is free to go gives the right answer and is far too slow to pass. The work has to come out proportional to the vertices and edges together, each edge accounted for a constant number of times.
objective: Recall and implement a linear-time topological ordering of a directed acyclic graph, including detecting that no ordering exists.
